I’ve farmed these flatlands of Quzhou County for more than forty years, and I know every mu of my eight-mu plot. With the education I received, I read the county’s agricultural bulletins and pay attention to market prices and weather patterns. Around here, the double-cropping system is still the most reliable way to make a living: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same patch of irrigated land. I’m not going to gamble with unfamiliar cash crops at my age; grain prices may not make me rich, but they pay the bills and the inputs are subsidized. This autumn I will sow an improved wheat variety—something like Jinmai or Jimai series that the extension station recommends for our saline-alkali soils. Come early June, right after the wheat harvest, I’ll plant Zhengdan 958 hybrid maize because it tolerates our summer heat and gives a steady yield. For wheat, I’ll do rotary tillage to break up the stubble from last year’s maize and level the seedbed. For maize, I’ve switched to no-tillage direct seeding after wheat harvest; it saves me three to five critical days in the narrow summer window and keeps moisture in the soil. On fertilizer, I follow the soil-test cards the county gives us: about fourteen kilograms of nitrogen per mu for wheat, a bit more for maize since it’s a heavier feeder, plus modest phosphorus and potassium. I irrigate wheat four times—sowing, overwintering, jointing, and grain filling—and maize twice if the summer rains fall short. I don’t spray chemicals blindly, but I will apply herbicide once and fungicide/insecticide once or twice when the extension service warns of aphid or rust pressure.
